Early Letters · recommended mark · round 3

Two voices, one large and one small.

An opening quotation mark, drawn once and set twice: the parent, and the child at 0.62 of its size, leaning in. It says the product's whole promise without a word. What follows is said exactly as you said it, to someone small.

Recommended: final A. Five independent critics reviewed it blind; the record and the open items are below.

Why this mark

It means the tagline

Quotation marks are the universal sign for words kept exactly as spoken. "Exactly as you said it" needs no caption.

Parent and child, by scale alone

No faces, hearts or babies. One mark is a scaled copy of the other, so the relationship carries the warmth.

Ownable in its category

The strategist found at least nine quote-mark icons on the App Store, all with marks of equal size. None used a large and small pair.

Three appearances
On a real home screen
Mark and wordmark

The wordmark is set in EB Garamond (SIL Open Font License), with the word space opened. The symbol aligns to the wordmark's ascender and sits 0.7 cap heights away. Its wedge ends echo the serifs.

At every size

A separate small cut with thicker tails and open notches is used at 40px and below. It only reaches a phone if the app ships an asset catalog with all sizes; that's an engineering task.

Alternative kept on file

Final B: the parent bends over

The large mark's tail arches over the child. It's the more ownable drawing and the warmer story. It's held back because at 16px the arch and the child start to merge, and the parent can read as a hooked 6 or a G. Worth putting in front of parents alongside A.

How we got here
Round 1

Two marks built on the letter e. You rejected both: an e communicates nothing.

Round 2

Six concepts from six designers: bedtime letter, two voices, a book that holds, years, kept note, a cot mobile. Five neutral critics reviewed them blind and found none at the bar.

  • The quotation marks were the strongest idea, ranked first by four of the five critics.
  • The moon reads as an Eid card.
  • The folded heart reads as broken.
  • The mobile is babyish and breaks when small.
Round 3

Two redraws, plus a test of the quotes placed on a letter. The letter version read as a document or a mail icon, so the pure pair won. The critics split 3 to 2: the crisper drawing felt more grown-up, the rounder one warmer and sturdier when small. The final merges the two: the crisp drawing at the rounder one's size and presence.

What the critics asked for, and what changed
Asked forDone in final A
No tadpole, sperm or cherry readShort, blunt tails with softened wedge ends. No curl.
Small mark is the true child of the largeOne drawing, scaled to 0.62, leaned 14 degrees toward the parent.
Never reads as the digits 66The child sits lifted and tilted toward the parent, not side by side.
Smooth joins, no bumpsCurvature-continuous joins; 14px corner radius on the tail cuts at 1024.
Bigger and centred in the tile56 percent of tile height (was 49), optically centred.
Gap that survives small sizes35px gap at 1024, plus a dedicated small cut at 40px and below.
Cleaner, less muddy tileDeeper, dithered gradient; the flat #8A5A3B is retired for the icon.
Still open
  • Final A or final B. My pick is A. A five-second recall test with about 20 parents at 60px and 29px would settle it for around $150 to $300 (a critic's estimate).
  • Trademark. No professional clearance search has been run. Register the specific drawing, not "quotation marks".
  • Device checks. Tinted light mode is the weakest appearance (about 3.8:1); check it and the gradient on a real iPhone.
  • On its own, the icon says "voice" more than "baby". The name and the subtitle "Baby memory book in your voice" carry that, which is normal for premium marks.
